title: Anatomical Terminology
shortDescription: The directional vocabulary every anatomy question is written in — superior, inferior, medial, lateral, and the rest, with paired examples.
genZNote: This is the app's directional "grammar" — get it wrong and every diagram question after it goes wrong too.

comparisons.distinction: Superior = toward the head/upper; inferior = toward the feet/lower.
Anterior (ventral) = toward the front; posterior (dorsal) = toward the back.
Medial = toward the body's midline; lateral = away from the midline.
Proximal = closer to the trunk/point of attachment; distal = farther from it (limb-specific terms).
Superficial = closer to the body surface; deep = farther from the surface.

questions.prompt: The elbow is ___ to the wrist.
questions.explanation: The elbow is closer to the trunk than the wrist, making it proximal to the wrist.
optionNotes: Distal would describe the wrist relative to the elbow, not the reverse.
Medial/lateral describe distance from the midline, not along a limb.
Superficial/deep describe depth, not position along a limb.

questions.prompt: True or False: A sagittal plane divides the body into anterior and posterior parts.
questions.explanation: False — a sagittal plane divides the body into left and right parts. The frontal (coronal) plane divides anterior and posterior.

questions.prompt: Which pair of terms describes nearness to the body surface, not up/down position?
questions.explanation: Superficial/deep describe depth relative to the body's surface, independent of up/down or front/back position.
optionNotes: Describes distance along a limb from the trunk.

sections.heading: Why Standard Terms Matter
sections.body: Words like "above" or "below" change meaning depending on body posture. Standard anatomical terms are always relative to the anatomical position, so a description stays accurate no matter how a person is actually lying or standing when examined.

rows: The heart is superior to the stomach.
The stomach is inferior to the heart.
The sternum is anterior to the spine.
The spine is posterior to the sternum.
Toward the midline of the body
The nose is medial to the eyes.
The eyes are lateral to the nose.
Closer to the point of attachment / trunk
The elbow is proximal to the wrist.
Farther from the point of attachment / trunk
The wrist is distal to the elbow.

sections.heading: Regional and Movement Terms (brief)
bullets: Axial region — head, neck, trunk (the body's main axis).
Appendicular region — the limbs (arms and legs) and their girdles.
Flexion — decreasing the angle at a joint; extension — increasing it.
Abduction — moving a limb away from the midline; adduction — moving it toward the midline.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Anatomical terminology is a fixed set of directional and regional terms, always defined relative to the standard anatomical position.
keyFacts: Proximal/distal are only used for limbs, relative to where they attach to the trunk.
Anterior = ventral, posterior = dorsal (the term pairs are interchangeable in most contexts).
Superficial/deep describe depth relative to the body surface, not up/down position.
commonConfusion: Medial/lateral are relative to the body's own midline, not to any other structure — the nose is medial regardless of which side of the face you compare it to.
Proximal and distal are frequently confused with superior/inferior — proximal/distal is specifically about distance from the trunk along a limb.

highYieldFacts: Anterior = ventral and posterior = dorsal are exact synonym pairs used interchangeably in exams.
"The elbow is ___ to the wrist" style fill-in-the-blank questions test proximal/distal specifically.
commonTraps: Don't apply proximal/distal to the trunk or head — they only make sense for limb structures.
"Superficial" does not mean "unimportant" in anatomy — it strictly means closer to the surface.
mustRemember: Ten paired terms: superior/inferior, anterior/posterior, medial/lateral, proximal/distal, superficial/deep.
All directional terms are defined relative to anatomical position, not the observer's own orientation.

confusedTerms.distinction: Medial is about nearness to the body's midline; proximal is about nearness to a limb's point of attachment to the trunk.
